```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
theme_set(theme_minimal())

# Causal graphs: letters in circles, one panel per value of `panel`. A circle's size is
# fixed on the page, in inches, while the figure's size decides how many inches a data
# unit is. draw_dag measures both on the graphics device open when it is called, and
# stops every arrow `gap` inches short of the circles.
draw_dag <- function(nodes, edges, xlim = c(-0.5, 2.5), ylim = c(-0.4, 1.4), gap = 0.05) {
  if (!"panel" %in% names(nodes)) { nodes$panel <- ""; edges$panel <- "" }
  dot <- 10; stroke <- 0.5; lw <- 0.5
  p <- ggplot() +
    geom_point(data = nodes, aes(x, y), size = dot, shape = 21, fill = "white", stroke = stroke) +
    geom_text(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = name), size = 4.5) +
    facet_wrap(~ panel, nrow = 1) +
    coord_fixed(xlim = xlim, ylim = ylim) +
    theme_void()
  # inches per data unit: the panels share what the strips and spacing leave of the figure
  inch <- function(u, f) f(u, "in", valueOnly = TRUE)
  g <- ggplotGrob(p)
  pp <- ggplot_build(p)$layout$panel_params[[1]]
  per_unit <- min((dev.size("in")[1] - sum(inch(g$widths, grid::convertWidth))) /
                    (length(unique(nodes$panel)) * diff(pp$x.range)),
                  (dev.size("in")[2] - sum(inch(g$heights, grid::convertHeight))) / diff(pp$y.range))
  # R draws a circle of radius 0.375 times its font size (shape 21); outline included
  r <- 0.375 * (dot * .pt + stroke * .stroke / 2) / 72 + stroke * .stroke / 2 / 96 / 2
  e <- edges |>
    left_join(nodes, by = c("panel", "from" = "name")) |> rename(x0 = x, y0 = y) |>
    left_join(nodes, by = c("panel", "to" = "name")) |>
    mutate(len = sqrt((x - x0)^2 + (y - y0)^2), ux = (x - x0) / len, uy = (y - y0) / len,
           # the end also clears half the line width, which the rounded tip adds
           s0 = (r + gap) / per_unit, s1 = (r + gap + lw * .pt / 96 / 2) / per_unit,
           xs = x0 + s0 * ux, ys = y0 + s0 * uy, xe = x - s1 * ux, ye = y - s1 * uy)
  p + geom_segment(data = e, aes(x = xs, y = ys, xend = xe, yend = ye),
                   arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.18, "cm"), type = "closed"), linewidth = lw)
}
```

## Discussion 1: absurd trolley problems

In your group, open
[Absurd Trolley Problems](https://neal.fun/absurd-trolley-problems/)
on one device and play for about six minutes, choosing together. Note
the scenarios where the group disagreed, and the ones you personally
found hard to choose.

1. Take one scenario where the group disagreed. Which framework was
   each side using?
2. Did any of your choices depend on a prediction of what would happen?
   How sure of it were you?

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Frameworks on the track" collapse="true"}
In the original problem, pulling the lever to save five people at the
cost of one is what a consequentialist who counts lives would do.
Refusing to pull it, because diverting the trolley makes you the cause
of one death while doing nothing lets five die, is one deontological
answer: it rests on a difference between doing and allowing. Other
deontologists allow pulling the lever, by the doctrine of double
effect: the one death is foreseen but not intended. A virtue ethicist
asks what a good person would do there, and can answer either way. Where a choice turned on a prediction, the consequentialist's
answer depended on a causal claim, and the game gives no way to check
it.
:::

## Discussion 2: a model that decides about people

Think of a scenario in which a predictive algorithm is deployed to make,
or help to make, decisions with large effects on people: which
applicants get a loan, which patients a GP sees first, which benefit
claims are checked for fraud. Choose one in your group.

1. Describe the scenario: who uses the model, what it predicts, from
   what data, and what is decided with it.
2. Decide what features or mechanisms would have to be in place to
   satisfy the four Belmont--Menlo principles and the five Cs (consent;
   clarity; consistency and trust; control and transparency;
   consequences). Say which principle or C each one serves.
3. Which of your requirements is about an effect, so that checking it
   needs a causal claim?

At the end, each group describes its scenario and its requirements to
the other groups.

::: {.callout-note .answer title="An example: suggestions for GPs" collapse="true"}
A model suggests treatments to NHS GPs, to help them get through
patient cases faster. It needs private information about each patient,
and may store it. It would need, among other things:

- informed consent from the patient, or from someone legally acting
  for them, to the use and storage of their data, and the data held
  securely or not at all (respect for persons; consent);
- a clear account to the patient of how the model is used, how their
  data is used and what happens to the data afterward (clarity;
  consistency and trust; beneficence);
- no use of the model for a patient who says no (control and
  transparency; beneficence);
- high accuracy, since a wrong suggestion can harm a patient
  (beneficence);
- a model that is demonstrably fair across demographic groups, since
  there are documented cases of medical algorithms biased by race or by
  sex (justice; consistency and trust);
- storage and processing that meet data-protection law such as the
  UK GDPR (respect for law and the public interest);
- care that its records cannot be combined with other sources to
  identify patients (consequences).

Accuracy is a property of the predictions. Whether patients do better
when their GP uses the suggestions than when the GP does not is an
effect, and that requirement needs a causal claim.
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="An example: checking benefit claims" collapse="true"}
A council uses a model to choose which housing-benefit claims its
officers check for fraud. The model was trained on the results of past
checks and uses each claim and other council records. It would need,
among other things:

- a notice to every claimant that a model helps choose which claims are
  checked, what data it uses and what a check involves (clarity;
  respect for persons). Consent is weak here, since a claimant cannot
  refuse and still claim, so the other requirements carry more weight;
- an officer who looks at each chosen claim before anything happens to
  it, so that the model only decides which claims are looked at
  (beneficence; respect for law and the public interest);
- check rates and error rates compared across groups, such as disabled
  claimants, single parents or claimants of one nationality, so that
  the burden of checks does not fall mostly on one group. The past
  checks the model learned from were themselves chosen by officers, so
  the model may learn to pick out the claimants they used to suspect
  (justice; consistency and trust);
- a way for claimants to see and correct the data used and to challenge
  a check, and a named officer who answers for the system (respect for
  law and the public interest; control and transparency);
- limits on joining other council records to the claims, and on what
  the results may be used for afterward (consequences).

Whether a check delays payments or causes hardship to honest
claimants, and whether checks deter fraud, are effects of the council's
choice to check, so those requirements need causal claims. Whether
flagged claims are more often fraudulent than claims chosen at random
is a question about the model's accuracy, and even that is hard to
measure, because few claims that were not flagged were ever checked.
:::

## Problems

Before you start, from memory: what does the adjustment formula
average, and with what weights?

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
It averages the outcome among people with $T = t$ within each group
defined by the adjustment variables, with weights equal to each
group's share of the whole population, not its share among the people
with $T = t$.
:::

### 1. A safety course for riders

A food-delivery platform offers its riders a road-safety course. It
pushes the course hardest to new riders and to riders who work mostly
at night. New riders have more accidents than experienced riders, by
day and by night, and night work raises accidents for both. New riders,
who book their shifts last, more often work at night. Assume that
nothing else affects both taking the course and having an accident.
The platform's records for 1,000 riders, with $Z = 1$ for a rider who
had joined in the three months before the course was offered, $W = 1$
for one who then worked mostly at night, $T = 1$ for one who took the
course and $Y = 1$ for one who had an accident in the six months
after:

| new ($Z$) | at night ($W$) | course ($T$) | riders | accidents |
|:---|:---|:---|---:|---:|
| yes | yes | yes | 70 | 21 |
| yes | yes | no | 30 | 12 |
| yes | no | yes | 100 | 10 |
| yes | no | no | 100 | 15 |
| no | yes | yes | 80 | 4 |
| no | yes | no | 120 | 18 |
| no | no | yes | 50 | 1 |
| no | no | no | 450 | 18 |

(a) Draw the graph with $T$, $Y$, $Z$ and $W$. Which set of variables
satisfies the backdoor criterion for the effect of $T$ on $Y$?

(b) Compute the share who had an accident among riders who took the
course and among those who did not.

(c) Compute $P(Y = 1 \mid do(T := 1))$ and $P(Y = 1 \mid do(T := 0))$
with the adjustment formula, and the average treatment effect.

(d) A manager proposes to drop the course, citing (b). An analyst who
adjusts only for whether riders are new finds that the course lowers
the chance of an accident by about 2.5 percentage points. What would
you tell each of them?

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
For (a), list the arrows into $T$. A set that blocks the paths that start with one of them can leave the paths that start with the other open.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Hint 2"}
For (c), find the share with an accident with and without the course in each of the four groups of riders, then weight each group by its share of all 1,000 riders.
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
(a) $Z \to W$, $Z \to T$, $W \to T$, $Z \to Y$, $W \to Y$ and
$T \to Y$.

```{r rider_graph, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.9, fig.width=3.4}
# W sits low and Z high, so that the arrowheads arriving at T and at Y stay apart
draw_dag(data.frame(name = c("T", "Y", "Z", "W"),
                    x = c(0, 2, 1, 1), y = c(0, 0, 1.9, 0.5)),
         data.frame(from = c("Z", "Z", "W", "Z", "W", "T"),
                    to = c("W", "T", "T", "Y", "Y", "Y")),
         xlim = c(-0.4, 2.4), ylim = c(-0.4, 2.3))
```

Two arrows point into $T$, and four backdoor paths start with them:
$T \leftarrow Z \to Y$, $T \leftarrow W \to Y$,
$T \leftarrow Z \to W \to Y$ and $T \leftarrow W \leftarrow Z \to Y$.
$\{Z, W\}$ blocks all four, and neither variable is a descendant of
$T$. $\{Z\}$ alone leaves $T \leftarrow W \to Y$ open, and $\{W\}$
alone leaves $T \leftarrow Z \to Y$ open. The graph rests on the
assumption in the question. If cautious riders were both more likely
to take the course and less likely to have an accident, caution would
be a back door that nobody measured.

(b) With the course: $(21 + 10 + 4 + 1)/(70 + 100 + 80 + 50) = 36/300 = 0.12$.
Without: $(12 + 15 + 18 + 18)/(30 + 100 + 120 + 450) = 63/700 = 0.09$.
Riders who took the course had an accident rate 3 points higher.

(c) Within each group of riders:

| new | at night | share of riders | with the course | without |
|:---|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| yes | yes | 0.1 | 21/70 = 0.30 | 12/30 = 0.40 |
| yes | no | 0.2 | 10/100 = 0.10 | 15/100 = 0.15 |
| no | yes | 0.2 | 4/80 = 0.05 | 18/120 = 0.15 |
| no | no | 0.5 | 1/50 = 0.02 | 18/450 = 0.04 |

$P(Y = 1 \mid do(T := 1)) = 0.1 \times 0.30 + 0.2 \times 0.10 + 0.2 \times 0.05 + 0.5 \times 0.02 = 0.07$
and
$P(Y = 1 \mid do(T := 0)) = 0.1 \times 0.40 + 0.2 \times 0.15 + 0.2 \times 0.15 + 0.5 \times 0.04 = 0.12$.
The average treatment effect is $-0.05$: the course lowers the chance
of an accident by 5 points. The sign of (b) is reversed because 83% of
the riders who took the course were new or worked at night, against
36% of those who did not, and those riders have more accidents with or
without the course.

(d) To the manager: riders who took the course had more accidents
because the platform gave it to the riders most likely to have one. In
every group the course lowers the rate. If the graph is right, the 300
riders who took it would have had about
$70 \times 0.40 + 100 \times 0.15 + 80 \times 0.15 + 50 \times 0.04 = 57$
accidents without it, against the 36 they had, so dropping it would
cost about 21 accidents in six months among riders like these. To the
analyst: adjusting for $Z$ alone leaves the back door through night
work, $T \leftarrow W \to Y$, open, and here that hides half the
effect. (Adjusting for $W$ alone hides nearly all of it.) The 5 points
and the 21 accidents rest on the graph; offering the course to riders
chosen at random would test it.
:::

### 2. Backdoor paths

In each graph, $T$ is the treatment and $Y$ the outcome.

```{r three_graphs, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.4, fig.width=8}
graphs <- c("Graph 1", "Graph 2", "Graph 3")
nodes <- data.frame(panel = rep(graphs, times = c(4, 5, 5)),
                    name = c("T", "Y", "A", "B", rep(c("T", "Y", "A", "B", "C"), 2)),
                    x = c(0, 2, 0.3, 1.7, rep(c(0, 2, 0.3, 1.7, 1), 2)),
                    y = c(0, 0, 1.3, 1.3, rep(c(0, 0, 1.3, 1.3, 0.7), 2)))
edges <- data.frame(panel = rep(graphs, times = c(4, 5, 7)),
                    from = c("A", "A", "B", "T",
                             "A", "A", "B", "B", "T",
                             "A", "A", "B", "B", "T", "C", "C"),
                    to = c("T", "B", "Y", "Y",
                           "T", "C", "C", "Y", "Y",
                           "T", "C", "C", "Y", "Y", "T", "Y"))
draw_dag(nodes, edges, xlim = c(-0.4, 2.4), ylim = c(-0.4, 1.7))
```

A path is blocked by a set of variables if somewhere along it

- a fork, $\leftarrow V \to$, or a chain, $\to V \to$ or
  $\leftarrow V \leftarrow$, has its middle variable $V$ in the set, or
- a collider, $\to V \leftarrow$, has neither $V$ nor any descendant of
  $V$ in the set.

The second rule is the reading's: a path through a collider is blocked
when you adjust for nothing, and adjusting for the collider opens it.

(a) For each graph, list the backdoor paths from $T$ to $Y$. Which of
them are open when you adjust for nothing?

(b) For each graph, find a smallest set of variables that satisfies the
backdoor criterion for the effect of $T$ on $Y$. Is it the only one of
that size?

(c) In graph 2, an analyst adjusts for $C$, because $C$ was measured
before $T$ and "adjusting for more can't hurt." Which path does that
open? Suppose $A$, $B$ and $C$ are yes-or-no variables, $A$ and $B$
are independent, and $A = 1$ or $B = 1$ is enough to make $C = 1$, as
either disease was enough for admission to hospital in the reading's
example. Among people with $C = 1$, are $A$ and $B$
associated, and in which direction?

(d) In graph 3, only $C$ was measured. Can the effect of $T$ on $Y$ be
estimated by adjusting for measured variables?

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
A backdoor path starts at $T$ with an arrow into $T$, then follows arrows in either direction to $Y$ without visiting a variable twice.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Hint 2"}
In graph 3, $C$ is on four backdoor paths. On which of them is it a collider?
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
(a) Graph 1: one, $T \leftarrow A \to B \to Y$, open. Graph 2: one,
$T \leftarrow A \to C \leftarrow B \to Y$, blocked, because $C$ is a
collider on it. Graph 3: four, $T \leftarrow C \to Y$,
$T \leftarrow A \to C \to Y$, $T \leftarrow C \leftarrow B \to Y$ and
$T \leftarrow A \to C \leftarrow B \to Y$. The first three are open;
the fourth is blocked at the collider $C$.

(b) Graph 1: $\{A\}$ or $\{B\}$. The path can be blocked anywhere along
it, so the common cause $A$ need not be measured if $B$ is. Graph 2:
the empty set. Any set without $C$ also works, such as $\{A\}$; a set
with $C$ and neither $A$ nor $B$ does not. Graph 3: $\{A, C\}$ or
$\{B, C\}$. Every set that blocks $T \leftarrow C \to Y$ contains $C$,
and adjusting for $C$ opens $T \leftarrow A \to C \leftarrow B \to Y$,
so $A$ or $B$ must be added to close it again. No single variable
works.

(c) It opens $T \leftarrow A \to C \leftarrow B \to Y$. Among people
with $C = 1$, $A$ and $B$ are negatively associated: among them,
those with $A = 0$ have $C = 1$ for some other reason, often $B$, so
$B = 1$ is more common among them than among those with $A = 1$. The
reading's two diseases
become negatively correlated among hospital patients in the same way.
So among people with $C = 1$, $T$ and $Y$ are associated through $A$
and $B$ even if $T$ does nothing, and adjusting for $C$ creates a bias
that the empty set did not have. If $A$ raises $T$ and $B$ raises $Y$,
the comparison within $C = 1$ is biased downward. Measured before $T$
does not mean safe to adjust for.

(d) No. The empty set leaves $T \leftarrow C \to Y$ open, and $\{C\}$
opens $T \leftarrow A \to C \leftarrow B \to Y$. Neither satisfies the
criterion. Adjusting for $C$ may still leave less bias than adjusting
for nothing; the graph alone does not say. To remove the bias, measure
$A$ or $B$, or assign $T$ at random.
:::

## Discussion 3: the case for one framework

The room splits into three groups. Each group develops an argument for
one statement and presents it to the other groups.

1. Ethical data science and AI development requires us to lean mostly
   on consequentialist ethics.
2. Ethical data science and AI development requires us to lean mostly
   on deontological ethics.
3. Ethical data science and AI development requires us to lean mostly
   on virtue ethics.

You have 15 minutes to develop your argument and 2 minutes to present
it. Think about how to structure it to convince the listener, and
answer the strongest objection to it. The group arguing for
consequentialism should also answer this question: does it become more
or less defensible once you have to write the causal model down?

Then everyone votes for the account they find most convincing, which
need not be the one their group argued for: consequentialist,
deontological or virtue ethics for data science and AI, a combination,
or none of them?

::: {.callout-note .answer title="An example: the case for consequentialism" collapse="true"}
Data science is used to make decisions at scale: who gets a loan, which
posts are shown, which claims are checked. Such a decision is judged by
what it does to the people it affects, added up over many cases, and
the field's own tools (outcomes, comparisons, trials) are built to
measure that. When every option harms someone, rules give no way to
weigh one harm against another, and the virtues of individual
employees say little about a system that no one person runs.

The strongest objection is that adding up outcomes lets a benefit to
many justify a serious harm to a few. The reply: count how the harms
and benefits are shared out, not only their total.

Writing the causal model down makes the position more defensible,
because its claims about consequences become explicit and open to
criticism. It also shows how much of any consequentialist case rests on
assumptions that the data cannot check, which is a strong argument
against it.
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="An example: the case for virtue ethics" collapse="true"}
Rules cannot anticipate every use of a model, and the consequences of a
new system can rarely be predicted well enough to add up. What is left
is the judgment of the people who build and run it. Virtue ethics asks
what kind of practitioner to be: honest about uncertainty, careful with
other people's data, willing to say no when a manager wants a
misleading result. Those are habits a team can train and a profession
can expect; the ASA's ethical guidelines, in the reading, ask
statisticians to be honest about the limits of their expertise.

The strongest objection is that "be honest and careful" gives no answer
in a hard case, such as whether to use a model that helps most
claimants and wrongly flags a few. The reply: no framework settles that case mechanically. A
consequentialist needs a causal model and a deontologist a ranking of
duties, and someone with good judgment has to supply both.
:::

## If there is time

- One sentence, individually: what is the difference between
  $P(Y = 1 \mid T = 1)$ and $P(Y = 1 \mid do(T := 1))$?
- The reading warns against judging an admissions test by how well it
  predicts success among the students who were admitted. Draw the
  graph. Where is the collider?
- "Correlation (more generally, association) is not causation." This
  is true and important, but can it be misused?
- Can causality be useful in the context of reproducibility? In
  designing and communicating studies?
- A company tests two versions of its app on its users, without telling
  them, to see which version keeps them using the app longer. Which of
  the Belmont--Menlo principles does this touch? How would each
  framework judge it?
- Find a sentence in a news report of an observational study that
  avoids saying "causes" but implies a cause. What graph does it
  assume?

Bring one score or algorithm used to make decisions about people. Write

### 3. Omitted-variable bias

In the linear model of the notes,
$Z := U_Z$, $X := \alpha Z + U_X$, $Y := \beta X + \gamma Z + U_Y$, with
independent mean-zero noise, take $\alpha = 2$, $\gamma = 1$,
$\beta = 0.5$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Z) = \operatorname{Var}(U_X) = 1$.

(a) Compute $\operatorname{Var}(X)$, $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Z)$ and the
slope of $Y$ on $X$ alone.

(b) Repeat with $\gamma = -1$.

(c) Repeat with $\gamma = 1$ and $\beta = 0$. What would someone with data
on $X$ and $Y$ alone conclude?

(d) Is the error in (a) a bias or a variance? What happens to it as the
sample grows?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
$Z$ and $U_X$ are independent, so $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \alpha^2 \operatorname{Var}(Z) + \operatorname{Var}(U_X)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
(a) $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 4 + 1 = 5$ and
$\operatorname{Cov}(X, Z) = \alpha \operatorname{Var}(Z) = 2$. The slope
is $\beta + \gamma \operatorname{Cov}(X, Z)/\operatorname{Var}(X) = 0.5 + 2/5 = 0.9$.

(b) $0.5 - 2/5 = 0.1$: the bias has the sign of $\gamma\alpha$, and here
it almost hides the effect.

(c) $0 + 2/5 = 0.4$. They would see a positive slope and could conclude
that raising $X$ raises $Y$, when intervening on $X$ does nothing.

(d) A bias. The slope converges to $0.9$ as the sample grows: the
estimates concentrate around $0.9$, not around the effect, $0.5$.
:::

### 4. Choosing an adjustment set

```{r five_nodes, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3, fig.width=5}
draw_dag(data.frame(name = c("Z", "X", "M", "Y", "W"),
                    x = c(1, 0, 1, 2, 2.9), y = c(1.1, 0, -0.6, 0, 1.1)),
         data.frame(from = c("Z", "Z", "X", "M", "X", "W"),
                    to = c("X", "Y", "M", "Y", "Y", "Y")),
         xlim = c(-0.5, 3.4), ylim = c(-0.9, 1.4))
```

(a) List the backdoor paths from $X$ to $Y$.

(b) Which of these sets satisfy the backdoor criterion: the empty set,
$\{Z\}$, $\{M\}$, $\{Z, M\}$, $\{W\}$, $\{Z, W\}$?

(c) In a linear model, what does the coefficient on $X$ estimate if you
adjust for $\{Z, M\}$?

(d) If more than one of the sets in (b) satisfies the criterion, which
would you use, and why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
A backdoor path starts with an arrow into $X$. How many arrows point into $X$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
(a) One: $X \leftarrow Z \to Y$.

(b) $\{Z\}$ and $\{Z, W\}$. The empty set and $\{W\}$ leave the back
door open. $\{M\}$ and $\{Z, M\}$ contain a descendant of $X$.

(c) The direct effect of $X$, along the arrow $X \to Y$: the part that
does not go through $M$. It is not the total effect of $X$. (It is the
direct effect because in this graph nothing else affects both $M$ and
$Y$.)

(d) $\{Z\}$ and $\{Z, W\}$ both satisfy it. Use $\{Z, W\}$: $W$ is not
a confounder, so leaving it out causes no bias, but it explains some of
the variation in $Y$, and the estimate that uses it is usually less
variable.
:::

### 5. The graph behind an argument

A university says: "Students who use the library more get better
grades. We will extend the library's opening hours, because using the
library improves grades."

(a) Draw the causal graph the argument presupposes, and mark the action.

(b) Add one variable that would make the observed difference larger
than the effect, with its arrows.

(c) What comparison would support the university's claim?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
The university's evidence compares students. Its action changes opening hours. Are those the same thing?
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
(a) Opening hours (the action) $\to$ library use $\to$ grades. The
argument needs the arrow from library use to grades, and an arrow from
opening hours to library use.

(b) For example motivation, or how well a student was already doing,
with arrows into library use and into grades. If it raises both, the
students who use the library more would have had better grades anyway,
so the observed difference is larger than the effect.

(c) Grades before and after the hours were extended, against a
comparable university or set of courses where they were not; or terms,
or sites, chosen at random to have longer hours. The comparison of
students who use the library more with those who use it less answers a
question about those students.
:::

### 6. Hormone therapy

The notes' section on hormone therapy and heart disease gives three
studies of whether to prescribe hormone therapy to prevent heart
disease.

(a) Write the decision with $X$ and $Y$. Say what the treatment and the
outcome are, and write the quantity a doctor needs with $do(\cdot)$.

(b) The 1996 estimate (0.39) and the 2008 estimates (1.42 over the first
two years, 0.96 over the whole follow-up) come from the same cohort.
Which comparison did each make?

(c) Draw a graph under which the 1996 estimate is confounded.

(d) Which comparison matches the decision a doctor makes, and why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
For (a), what does the doctor choose, and which outcome is the choice about? For (b), ask which two groups each analysis compares.
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
(a) $X = 1$ if the doctor prescribes hormone therapy, $Y = 1$ if the
woman has coronary heart disease within five years.
A doctor needs $P(Y = 1 \mid do(X := 1))$ against
$P(Y = 1 \mid do(X := 0))$, not $P(Y = 1 \mid X = 1)$ against
$P(Y = 1 \mid X = 0)$.

(b) 1996: women who took estrogen with progestin against women who did
not use hormones, adjusted for measured confounders. 2008: women who
started against women who did not start, both followed from the same
point, analyzed as the trial was.

(c) Socioeconomic status $\to$ hormone use, socioeconomic status $\to$
heart disease, with or without an arrow from hormone use to heart
disease.

(d) The 2008 comparison. The doctor's decision is whether to start,
and that comparison follows women from the point at which they started
or did not.
:::

### Coding

Open a fresh R script. You will need the tidyverse.

#### A. Prediction and intervention

```{r coding_a_setup}
n <- 10000
# program 1: X causes Y
X1 <- rnorm(n); Y1 <- 2 * X1 + rnorm(n)
# program 2: Z causes both
Z2 <- rnorm(n); X2 <- Z2 + rnorm(n); Y2 <- Z2 + rnorm(n)
# program 3: X causes Y through M
X3 <- sqrt(2) * rnorm(n); M3 <- X3 + sqrt(2) * rnorm(n); Y3 <- 0.5 * M3 + rnorm(n)
```

1. Write down the slope of $Y$ on $X$ you expect in each program. Then
   fit `lm` and compare.
2. For each program, intervene: set $X$ to 1 for everyone and run the
   statements after the one for $X$ again, then the same with $X$ set
   to 0. Compute the difference in the means of $Y$.
3. In program 2, fit `lm(Y2 ~ X2 + Z2)`. In program 3, fit
   `lm(Y3 ~ X3 + M3)`. Compare the coefficients on $X$ with your
   answers to 2.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
In each program, which statements after the one for $X$ use $X$, directly or through a variable computed from it? Those are the ones whose values change when you set $X$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
```{r coding_a_solution}
slopes <- c(coef(lm(Y1 ~ X1))[2], coef(lm(Y2 ~ X2))[2], coef(lm(Y3 ~ X3))[2])
do1 <- c(mean(2 * 1 + rnorm(n)),                    # X set to 1, later statements re-run
         mean(Z2 + rnorm(n)),
         mean(0.5 * (1 + sqrt(2) * rnorm(n)) + rnorm(n)))
do0 <- c(mean(2 * 0 + rnorm(n)),                    # X set to 0
         mean(Z2 + rnorm(n)),
         mean(0.5 * (0 + sqrt(2) * rnorm(n)) + rnorm(n)))
round(rbind(slope = slopes, effect = do1 - do0), 2)
round(coef(lm(Y2 ~ X2 + Z2))[2], 2)    # program 2, adjusting for Z
round(coef(lm(Y3 ~ X3 + M3))[2], 2)    # program 3, adjusting for M
```
The slopes are about 2, 0.5 and 0.5. The effects are about 2, 0 and
0.5. In programs 2 and 3, $X$ and $Y$ have the same joint distribution
(jointly normal, with means 0, variances 2 and 2 and covariance 1), so $X$ predicts
$Y$ equally well in both, and intervening on $X$ changes $Y$ only in
program 3. Adjusting for $Z$ in program 2 gives a coefficient near 0,
the effect. Adjusting for $M$ in program 3 also gives a coefficient
near 0. That is the direct effect, zero here because $X$ reaches $Y$
only through the mediator $M$; the total effect is 0.5.
:::

#### B. Adjustment on data

The table of problem 1, one row for each rider.

```{r coding_b_setup}
cells <- data.frame(Z = c(1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0),
                    W = c(1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0),
                    T = c(1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0),
                    n = c(70, 30, 100, 100, 80, 120, 50, 450),
                    accidents = c(21, 12, 10, 15, 4, 18, 1, 18))
# In base R, T means TRUE; inside dplyr verbs, T is the column
riders <- bind_rows(
  cells |> mutate(Y = 1, count = accidents),
  cells |> mutate(Y = 0, count = n - accidents)
) |>
  select(Z, W, T, Y, count) |>
  tidyr::uncount(count)
nrow(riders)
```

1. Compute the share with an accident among riders who took the course
   and among those who did not, from `riders`, and the difference.
2. Compute the adjusted difference: the difference within each
   combination of $Z$ and $W$, averaged with weights $P(Z = z, W = w)$.
   Then adjust for $Z$ alone, and for $W$ alone.
3. A randomized version: give each of the 1,000 riders the course with
   probability 0.3, whatever their group, and draw whether they have an
   accident from the table's rates. Compute the difference. Repeat 200
   times. What is the average difference, and how much does it vary?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
For 2: `riders |> group_by(Z, W) |> summarize(...)` gives one row for each group of riders; compute the difference and the group's share of all riders there.
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
```{r coding_b_solution}
riders |> group_by(T) |> summarize(rate = mean(Y))

adjusted <- function(...) {
  rows <- riders |>
    group_by(...) |>
    summarize(diff = mean(Y[T == 1]) - mean(Y[T == 0]),
              share = n() / nrow(riders), .groups = "drop")
  sum(rows$diff * rows$share)
}
round(c(both = adjusted(Z, W), Z_only = adjusted(Z), W_only = adjusted(W)), 3)

rates <- riders |> group_by(Z, W, T) |> summarize(rate = mean(Y), .groups = "drop")
groups <- cells |> group_by(Z, W) |> summarize(n = sum(n), .groups = "drop")
one_trial <- function() {
  trial <- groups |>
    tidyr::uncount(n) |>
    mutate(T = rbinom(n(), 1, 0.3)) |>
    left_join(rates, by = c("Z", "W", "T")) |>
    mutate(Y = rbinom(n(), 1, rate))
  mean(trial$Y[trial$T == 1]) - mean(trial$Y[trial$T == 0])
}
trials <- replicate(200, one_trial())
c(mean = mean(trials), sd = sd(trials))
```
1. 0.12 and 0.09, a difference of 0.03.

2. $-0.05$ with both. With $Z$ alone about $-0.025$, and with $W$ alone
about $-0.001$: each leaves one back door open.

3. The average is close to $-0.05$, and the differences vary from trial
to trial with a standard deviation of about 0.02. Randomization removes
the bias without measuring $Z$ or $W$, and the price is that a single
trial can miss by a few points.
:::

#### C. Intervening in a program

The job center from the lecture, as a program. As in the lecture,
everyone referred attends and nobody else does. Each line generates one
variable from the ones above it.

```{r course_starter, eval=FALSE}
n <- 10000
Z <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)                        # worked last year
X <- rbinom(n, 1, ifelse(Z == 1, 0.8, 0.2))   # attended the course
Y <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.3 + 0.1 * X + 0.3 * Z)    # in work six months later
mean(Y[X == 1]) - mean(Y[X == 0])             # attenders against the others
```

1. Run it. Compare the difference with the lecture's first job-center table (64% against 36%).
2. Compute the adjusted difference: the difference between attenders
   and non-attenders within $Z = 1$ and within $Z = 0$, averaged with
   weights `mean(Z == 1)` and `mean(Z == 0)`.
3. Intervene. Replace the line for `X` by `X <- rep(1, n)`, run the
   line for `Y` again, and record `mean(Y)`. Do the same with
   `X <- rep(0, n)`. Compare the difference with your answer to 2.
4. The center changes its referrals to 0.95 for $Z = 1$ and 0.05 for
   $Z = 0$. Before you run anything, write down what you expect for the
   differences in 1 and in 3. Then run it.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
For step 3, replace the line for `X` and leave the line for `Z` alone. Then run the line for `Y` again, so that it uses the new `X`.
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
```{r course_solution}
set.seed(313)    # the sheet's seed, so this output does not depend on the chunks above it
n <- 10000
Z <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
X <- rbinom(n, 1, ifelse(Z == 1, 0.8, 0.2))
Y <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.3 + 0.1 * X + 0.3 * Z)
observed <- mean(Y[X == 1]) - mean(Y[X == 0])
d1 <- mean(Y[X == 1 & Z == 1]) - mean(Y[X == 0 & Z == 1])   # within Z = 1
d0 <- mean(Y[X == 1 & Z == 0]) - mean(Y[X == 0 & Z == 0])   # within Z = 0
adjusted <- d1 * mean(Z == 1) + d0 * mean(Z == 0)
Y1 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.3 + 0.1 * 1 + 0.3 * Z)    # everyone attends
Y0 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.3 + 0.1 * 0 + 0.3 * Z)    # nobody attends
c(observed = observed, adjusted = adjusted, intervened = mean(Y1) - mean(Y0))

X95 <- rbinom(n, 1, ifelse(Z == 1, 0.95, 0.05))
Y95 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.3 + 0.1 * X95 + 0.3 * Z)
mean(Y95[X95 == 1]) - mean(Y95[X95 == 0])      # observed, new referrals
```
1. About $0.28$, the table's $0.64 - 0.36$.

2. About $0.10$.

3. About $0.10$: intervening deletes the arrow $Z \to X$, and the
adjusted difference estimates the same quantity.

4. The observed difference grows to about
$(0.95 \times 0.7 + 0.05 \times 0.4) - (0.05 \times 0.6 + 0.95 \times 0.3) = 0.685 - 0.315 = 0.37$.
The effect of the course stays at $0.10$: the referral policy changes
who attends, not what the course does. Each run differs from these
numbers by a few hundredths.
:::
